newsitem.title: KENYA: African leaders gather to review Burundi embargo.
newsitem.headline: African leaders gather to review Burundi embargo.

text.p: Regional African leaders gathered in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha on Tuesday to review the crippling economic embargo imposed on war-torn and ethnically divided Burundi in July.

Ambassadors from Ethiopia, Rwanda, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Zambia, Zaire and officials from the organisation of African Unity (OAU) are meeting ahead of a foreign ministers summit on Thursday and a presidential one on Saturday, officials said.
The ambassadorial committee will review policy and decide if Burundi's military junta led by Major Pierre Buyoya has done enough to warrant an easing of the sanctions.

"The committee will work out recommendations on whether the sanctions should be eased, lifted altogether or even tightened further," an ambassador at the one-day talks told Reuters by telephone from Arusha.
"These recommendations will then be passed on to the committee of foreign ministers and eventually the heads of state on Saturday for ratification," added another official at the Arusha meeting.
Diplomats said few details still needed to be sorted out on Saturday's meeting of heads of state.

First, Buyoya needs to receive and accept an invitation to the summit. Tanzanian government officials said Tanzania would like Buyoya to attend as a faction leader and not head of state while Buyoya insists on attending only in his capacity as president.
"These issues will have to be sorted out otherwise the meeting will go ahead without him in which case little progress can be expected from the meeting," one official said.

Burundi says the sanctions cost it more than $130 million in the first two months. Worst-hit are the workers and residents of Bujumbura, an eerie town abandoned by majority Hutus who have fled to the countryside.
Buyoya's junta last month unbanned political parties, restored parliament and agreed in principle to meet Hutu rebels, waging a ferocious war aid workers say is killing up to 1,000 people monthly.

In so doing, Buyoya and his military colleagues believe they have gone far enough in responding to demands imposed by regional countries after Buyoya overthrew the government of Hutu president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya.

But leaders from the main Hutu rebel group -- the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD), which has stepped up its fight for a larger political stake in Burundi -- told Reuters on Tuesday that Buyoya's moves were not enough to warrant direct talks between the two sides.
"Buyoya has not done enough and we shall therefore not be talking to him," said Innocent Nimpagaritse, CNDD East Africa representative.
The war in Burundi, pitting the country's Tutsi-dominated army against Hutu rebels, has claimed more than 150,000 lives in the past three years including a president and an archbishop.
Analysts fear Burundi could go down the same path as neighbouring Rwanda, where a million Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus were slaughtered in 1994.
